transcript:
Meeting header:
- Date/Time: 2025-06-17 11:30 PT
- Duration: ~58 minutes
- Location: Zoom
- Attendees: Jordan, Priya, Mateo (Redwood) | Alex, Samira, Devon, Taylor (OptimaEdge)

Auto Summary (auto-gen, may be rough): Customer sees spiky tail latencies during marketing-driven traffic bursts; exploring scheduler knob sets, token limits, and caching adjustments to smooth throughput while preserving latency SLOs.

[00:00:00] Jordan (Redwood AE): Okay everyone, thanks for joining. Quick roll call — and then Priya will jump into the perf telemetry you shared.
[00:00:14] Alex (OptimaEdge): Hey all, Alex here. We've got a 2pm daily spike where p95 jumps and some requests hit 800-900ms, sometimes 1.2s.
[00:00:28] Priya (Redwood SE): Got it. I pulled the logs you uploaded — thanks — and the burst is short, like 3-7 minutes, but very dense in concurrency. Looks like a lot of mid-length generations 150-400 tokens.
[00:00:42] Samira (ML Eng): Yeah we do a lot of multi-turn assistant prompts during campaigns. We haven't capped tokens aggressively.
[00:00:50] Mateo (Redwood): First question, are you on hosted or private? That changes recommended knobs.
[00:00:55] Alex: We're on private (VPC deployment) with a 4-node GPU pool, nv4x instances, dedicated.
[00:01:05] Jordan: Perfect. So we can adjust runtime knobs and quantization more freely. Priya, can you summarize the telemetry graph?
[00:01:12] Priya: Sure. I see two failure modes during spikes: one is scheduler saturation — queue depth spikes and packing_window_ms expands because the runtime is trying to assemble bigger batches — that increases tail. The other is token-guard backpressure where a few long contexts block max_num_seqs slots.
[00:01:36] Taylor (SRE): When you say max_num_seqs, is that global per GPU or per worker thread?
[00:01:42] Priya: In our runtime there are two levels. max_num_seqs is an upper bound on the number of concurrently active sequences per model instance (essentially per-GPU slot pool). There's also packing_bucket limits that affect how many sequences can be packed into one kernel call.
[00:01:58] Devon (Platform): We're seeing the packing_window_ms default at 25ms. Should we shrink it?
[00:02:03] Priya: Shrinking to 10ms reduces latency but lowers batch sizes, so throughput drops and cost per token rises. There's a tradeoff. For peak bursts that are short and super-concurrent, a smaller window can keep p95 down if you accept slightly higher cost.
[00:02:20] Alex: Our p50 is fine, but p95 and p99 during the 5-minute blast are scary. We'd rather keep p95 under 400ms.
[00:02:28] Priya: Understood. Proposed plan: two knob sets to test. Set A: packing_window_ms=10ms, max_num_seqs reduced by 20% to avoid long-context blocking, token_guard_threshold=1200 tokens, enforce per-request max_tokens=600. Set B: packing_window_ms=30ms, enable priority_preemption for short requests, increase max_num_seqs by 10% and add a soft token quota for long contexts. We'll bench both with your real traffic.
[00:02:55] Jordan: Note, priority_preemption lets short low-token requests skip ahead of long ones in the scheduler — helps tail. But preemption causes some context switches which affect throughput.
[00:03:07] Samira: How does KV cache interplay here? Our prompts have a lot of shared prefixes across sessions.
[00:03:12] Priya: Good point. If you have high prefix reuse, enabling prefix-based KV cache (we call it prefix-compact caching) will raise hit rate and reduce compute by avoiding repeated attention work. During bursts KV hit-rate improvements can effectively reduce active seqs. However, cold-starts at the beginning of a campaign will still spike.
[00:03:30] Alex: We saw KV hit-rate only 18% during spikes. Any quick wins?
[00:03:34] Priya: Two: increase cache size for short-term entries (TTL), and pre-populate likely prefixes before the marketing blast (warm cache) — Redwood can accept a preload API call set. Also adjust kv_hitrate_threshold for eviction to be more conservative during peak windows.
[00:03:50] Devon: Preloading is doable. We'll generate the likely prefixes from logs.
[00:03:55] Jordan: Let's talk quantization — you're on Ampere GPUs, is that correct?
[00:04:00] Alex: A100s.
[00:04:02] Mateo: With A100s we can run q4_0 or int8 profiles. q4_0 tends to give good perf uplift with minimal quality drop for many assistant tasks; int8 can be riskier for hallucination but faster. For private pools we can deploy a mixed profile: q4 for most routes, int8 for low-precision internal rerank workloads.
[00:04:20] Samira: Concerned about quality regression during customer-facing outputs.
[00:04:24] Priya: Then start with q4 and measure eval metrics on your sample prompts. Redwood Optimize has a small eval harness we can run. Mateo will share the harness link.
[00:04:33] Alex: Thanks. Back to scheduler knobs: you mentioned token_guard_threshold. Is that the same as per-request token cap?
[00:04:38] Priya: Slight difference. token_guard_threshold is a scheduler-level signal that prevents extremely long contexts from monopolizing a slot. per-request max_tokens enforces a hard limit on generation length. Use both: soft guard to shape scheduling, hard cap as last resort.
[00:04:52] Taylor: If we enforce per-request caps, some of our internal async workflows that expect longer continuations will break. Any way to do exceptions?
[00:04:59] Priya: Yes — create a priority class for trusted internal clients and route them to a separate instance or set different knob overrides (e.g., higher max_num_seqs, larger packing buckets).
[00:05:10] Jordan: We should also instrument token consumption per-account; Redwood Console can show token burn by API key to identify heavy contexts.
[00:05:17] Alex: Great. Does continuous_batching=true change anything here?
[00:05:21] Priya: Continuous batching smooths throughput by keeping GPU kernels fed with micro-batches; it's great when requests are frequent. But for peaky, bursty traffic that comes in a short window, continuous batching can create longer assembly latencies if packing_window_ms is large. So continuous batching + small packing windows + priority preemption is a useful combo.
[00:05:39] Samira: Are there knobs to limit how many tokens a single tenant can occupy across the pool?
[00:05:44] Mateo: We have tenant_token_quota and tenant_seq_quota. tenant_token_quota is useful to prevent one customer loop from consuming most GPU cycles during a blast. For a single-tenant private pool you may use tenant_seq_quota to restrict per-client sessions; for multi-tenant it's essential.
[00:05:58] Alex: We're single-tenant, though many internal teams. We can use priority classes instead of tenant quota then.
[00:06:03] Priya: Right. Set priority_class for high SLO teams, default for others. Also configure a fallback model (lighter quantized variant) for overflow. Redwood runtime supports automatic fallback when pool is saturated.
[00:06:16] Taylor: That automatic fallback — is it per-request or per-route?
[00:06:19] Jordan: Per-route policy. You can say: if latency exceeds X or queue depth > Y, route to q4 variant or to a staged smaller model. Works nicely to preserve availability.
[00:06:28] Devon: We saw a config where fallback increased p95 because the smaller model took longer for some prompts. Any guidance?
[00:06:34] Priya: Test fallback on your representative prompts. For many completions q4 variants actually reduce latency. But for complex chain-of-thought prompts, fallback can increase latency. That's why we recommend pairing fallback with a route-level filter: only route short-token requests to fallback, or use content-aware routing if you can tag requests.
[00:06:52] Alex: Ok. For the bench, what's required input from us?
[00:06:56] Priya: A 3-6 hour trace of production traffic covering a peak, sanitized. Prefer CSV with timestamp, latency, prompt_length, response_length, client_id. We'll replay at realistic concurrency and rate patterns.
[00:07:09] Alex: We'll export that.
[00:07:11] Jordan: Let's sketch the two bench configs again for clarity. Priya?
[00:07:15] Priya: Set A (latency-first): continuous_batching=true, packing_window_ms=10, max_num_seqs = current * 0.8, per-request max_tokens=600, priority_preemption=off, preload_kv=true. Set B (throughput-first with tail mitigation): continuous_batching=true, packing_window_ms=30, max_num_seqs = current * 1.1, priority_preemption=on with preemption_threshold=150 tokens, tenant_seq_quota=65% for low-priority teams, fallback_model=q4_0. We'll run both and produce p50/p95/p99, throughput (tokens/s), and cost estimate.
[00:08:01] Samira: How do we measure KV cache effectiveness in the bench?
[00:08:04] Priya: We instrumented KV hits per request in the runtime. Bench will report kv_hitrate, and we can run a warm vs cold scenario (preload vs no preload) to quantify delta.
[00:08:14] Taylor: Any network considerations for VPC? We saw some packet drops during the blast which may aggravate tail.
[00:08:19] Mateo: Right — on-prem/VPC networking is critical. If control-plane calls, KMS/HSM, or S3 fetches block the runtime during peak, you'll see elevated tail. We recommend colocating model weights on local NVMe and ensuring KMS latency is <50ms. Also disable sync checkpoints during peak windows.
[00:08:37] Devon: We do periodic weight reloads every 15 minutes; maybe that's colliding.
[00:08:40] Priya: If reloads overlap with a marketing blast, they will hurt. Shift reloads to off-peak or throttle them.
[00:08:46] Jordan: A few notes on observability: Redwood Console can add route-level tracing to show kernel-level occupancy, sequence counts, packing_window histograms, and token burn per API key. That will help validate the bench and the choice of max_num_seqs.
[00:09:02] Alex: Good. If we choose Set A and it's too costly, can we gate it only during the blast windows?
[00:09:08] Priya: Yes — time-based policy overrides are supported. You can have an on-call schedule or a cron-style window to switch knob profiles.
[00:09:15] Samira: One more on preemption: what's the overhead when a request is preempted?
[00:09:19] Priya: Minimal for short requests, but there is a small requeue cost measured in microseconds to a few ms; the bigger cost is if long contexts have primed KV and then get evicted — that can reduce hit-rate briefly. We attempt to preserve KV entries for preempted owners where feasible.
[00:09:36] Devon: For tests, what's a meaningful p99 target?
[00:09:39] Jordan: Depends on your SLO. You mentioned p95 < 400ms; p99 often sits 2-3x p95 for highly variable bursts. A realistic p99 goal after tuning might be under 1s for your workload with these knob sets.
[00:09:51] Alex: Acceptable.
[00:09:53] Priya: Quick note on max_num_seqs: lowering it prevents long-running contexts from creating head-of-line blocking, but if set too low you underutilize GPU and cost increases. The bench will show the utilization curve; look for the knee where utilization flattens and tail improves.
[00:10:08] Mateo: Also watch for max_tokens_per_call and token batching behaviour — some customers send many small responses that pack well, others send fewer long responses that need different tuning.
[00:10:19] Taylor: Are there recommended defaults for A100 private pools?
[00:10:22] Priya: For A100 private pools: packing_window_ms 15-25ms, continuous_batching=true, max_num_seqs tuned to 60-120 depending on model size and seq length distribution, token_guard_threshold ~1200-1800 tokens. But these are starting points.
[00:10:39] Alex: Our median seq length is 180, average response length 220 tokens.
[00:10:45] Priya: Then start with max_num_seqs ~85 and run the bench.
[00:10:49] Jordan: Let's capture risk areas: KV cold-starts, weight reload collisions, and KMS latency. Mateo, add those to your note.
[00:10:56] Mateo: Will do.
[00:10:58] Samira: A bit of noise in the telemetry looked like the runtime reported 'k v' as separate events — any artifact?
[00:11:03] Priya: Sometimes transcribers capture k-v as 'k v' but runtime logs are fine. We'll parse logs and send a cleaned CSV.
[00:11:10] Alex: For preloading, what's the API pattern?
[00:11:13] Jordan: You can call the preload endpoint with a list of prefixes or session IDs. We'll include example script in the follow-up.
[00:11:20] Priya: Alright, should we go into the bench plan timeline?
[00:11:24] Alex: Yes please.
[00:11:26] Priya: We'll run a 3-hour bench for each config (A and B) — two runs each for warm and cold cache conditions. So 4 runs total. We'll provide p50/p95/p99, tokens/s, kv_hitrate, avg_gpu_util, and cost estimate. Expect results by end of day 2025-06-20.
[00:11:45] Devon: Will Redwood need elevated access into our cluster?
[00:11:48] Jordan: No, we run the bench from your image via agent you run in your environment. We'll provide a small agent and instructions — no persistent access.
[00:11:57] Taylor: Good. One more thing: we use an internal reranker that makes short high-frequency calls upstream. Any special handling?
[00:12:03] Priya: Rerankers are perfect candidates for priority_preemption + dedicated route with small packing_window. That reduces their tail and prevents interfering with longer completion flows.
[00:12:14] Samira: If we enable priority_preemption for reranker, will it always preempt or only when queue depth is high?
[00:12:19] Priya: You set the preemption policy. We recommend 'preempt_when_queue_depth>Y' so it activates during congestion only.
[00:12:28] Jordan: We're at 12 minutes in; any other big questions?
[00:12:33] Alex: Not yet. Let's fast-forward to instrumentation plan.
[00:12:36] Priya: Instrumentation checklist: enable route-level kernel occupancy traces, enable sequence_count_histograms, enable kv_hitrate logging, attach CPU/GPU utilization from node exporter, and collect network p99 for KMS and S3. We'll provide the prometheus dashboard JSON and Redwood Console overlay.
[00:12:54] Devon: Ok we'll add the exporters.
[00:12:56] Mateo: Quick note: if you opt for mixed quantization we recommend stage rollout — run A/B on a small percentage of traffic to watch hallucination/regression. Redwood Optimize can automatically compute small eval deltas.
[00:13:11] Alex: We'll do that.
[00:13:14] Priya: Any concerns about pricing impact of Set A? It will be higher cost due to lower amortized GPU efficiency. We'll estimate cost delta in the bench report.
[00:13:23] Alex: Budget is flexible for 2 hours around the blast if it keeps customer experience good.
[00:13:28] Jordan: Great. Next steps recap: Alex to upload trace by 2025-06-19, Priya to run bench and share artifacts by 2025-06-20, follow-up call week of 2025-06-23. Mateo to share quantization/Optimize links and preload script.
[00:13:46] Samira: One last question: any runtime flags we should avoid changing during peak?
[00:13:50] Priya: Avoid changing model weight reload frequency, and avoid toggling global cache eviction policies live — those are disruptive. Use time-window overrides instead.
[00:14:01] Jordan: Alright, thanks everyone. We'll post the meeting notes and plug in the next call.
[00:14:07] Alex: Thanks all.
[00:14:10] (wrap up, short side-channel clarifications, some crosstalk)
